newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam sidesteps U.S. charges of media clampdown.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam sidesteps U.S. charges of media clampdown.

text.p: Vietnam's ruling Communist Party lashed out on Thursday at U.S. radio stations over criticism of its record on press freedoms and said improvements in the quality and quantity of domestic media were being ignored.

A commentary in the party mouthpiece Nhan Dan daily accused the Voice of America and other U.S. broadcasters of orchestrating a "human rights concerto" against Vietnam, and asked rhetorically whether this would help bilateral relations.
"What is the purpose of such propaganda cooked up by these radio stations when Vietnam-U.S. relations are being improved, opening more prospects for mutual understanding?" it said.

"No one can deny the recent positive socio-economic changes in Vietnam. The Communist Party and Government of Vietnam have exerted great efforts to help the people... actually enjoy rights to freedom and democracy, including freedom of the press."
The commentary went on to detail a media proliferation in Vietnam over the past 10 years and said this had been matched by corresponding improvements in quality.
"It seems that you have no goodwill, you take part in a concerto of human rights, and try to sell a product that nobody wants to buy," it added.

Vietnam's media has expanded in numerical terms since reforms were launched in the late 1980s. According to the Nhan Dan commentary, some 562 press publications today are complimented by numerous local TV and radio stations.

But in recent months foreign and domestic commentators have claimed a press clampdown, with closer state monitoring of journalists, their contacts, and activities, alongside imposition of restrictive new foreign press rules.
According to Communist Party policy Vietnam's domestic media remains primarily a tool of state propaganda. Foreign journalists are normally allowed to operate without explicit censorship.
The press freedoms issue is nonetheless a sore point for Hanoi, which expelled a resident U.S. journalist in November last year after criticising him for reporting negatively.
The incident was included in a U.S. State Department report on human rights in Vietnam issued earlier this year, which also noted other infringements against members of the press.
